content:
Understanding the role of motivation in engaging students in laboratory skill education is essential for enhancing learning outcomes and academic achievement. Physical science laboratories are widely regarded as experiential learning environments in which students develop advanced conceptual understanding and procedural skills. Students’ attitudes toward these laboratories directly influence the effectiveness of skill training.

In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, computer-based virtual laboratories (VLs) emerged as a viable alternative for conducting skill training and experimental activities under lockdown and social distancing constraints. Despite their potential, the adoption of VLs has remained limited, largely due to insufficient awareness and familiarity among both teachers and students.

This study investigated the key motivational factors that influence the effectiveness of VLs in teaching laboratory skills and procedures. Data were collected through a survey-based design, employing the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI) to measure students’ intrinsic motivation, self-reported survey items to assess relevant extrinsic factors, and a teacher perception scale to capture instructors’ views of VLs. Independent-samples t-tests and automatic linear modeling (LINEAR) were used to analyze the data.

The findings indicate that animated graphical learning materials in VLs have a stronger positive effect on students’ intrinsic motivation than traditional e-book–based materials. The results also underscore the critical role of teachers in fostering students’ motivation to conduct laboratory experiments using VLs. Furthermore, repeated or extended engagement with VL experiments—either through longer sessions or multiple practice attempts—was found to positively influence students’ laboratory performance.
